activities.anchor: Abstract algebra does something that looks like madness
activities.caption: group or not?
activities.name: aaGroupSort

config.prompt: Which of these systems are groups under the stated operation? Check closure, identity, inverses and associativity.

items.label: hours on a clock, addition mod 12

config.why: A group needs closure, an identity, inverses and associativity. Natural numbers lack 0 and negatives; odd integers fail closure; the others satisfy all four.

activities.anchor: The school definitions — point, line, angle, parallel
activities.caption: call the spherical angle sum
activities.name: aaSphereEst

config.prompt: On a sphere, a triangle runs from the North Pole to the equator, a quarter of the way round, and back. Its three angles are all right angles. What is the angle sum?
config.why: 90° + 90° + 90° = 270°. The 90° excess over 180° is proportional to the triangle's area — the foundation of spherical trigonometry.
config.context: on a flat plane the sum would be exactly 180°

activities.anchor: deserves its own attention as the template
activities.caption: fill the blanks — the axiomatic contract
activities.name: aaEuclidCloze

config.text: Euclid's Elements organises geometry as %%0%% definitions, %%1%% postulates and %%2%% propositions, each proved only from what came before.
config.hint: The numbers are 23, 5 and 465 — the count of propositions is the surprising one.

activities.anchor: Similar figures (E4.4) differ by a scale factor k
activities.caption: call the model's area
activities.name: aaScaleEst

config.prompt: A 1:20 architectural model is built of a 15 m × 10 m room. What area does the model cover?
config.why: The real area is 150 m²; areas scale as k², so the model is 150 / 20² = 150 / 400 = 0.375 m².
config.context: lengths scale by 20, areas by 400, volumes by 8,000

activities.caption: pair each figure with its symmetry count
activities.name: aaSymMatch

config.prompt: Pair each figure with its number of symmetries (identity included):

pairs.left: parallelogram that is not a rectangle

config.why: Symmetries compose as a group. The non-square rectangle has two reflections and a 180° rotation plus the identity; the generic parallelogram keeps only the identity and the half-turn.

activities.caption: mark the spherical triangle's angle sum
activities.name: aaAnglePlace

config.prompt: A spherical triangle has angle sum 270°. Place that sum on the angle axis.
config.why: The sum exceeds 180° by 90° — the spherical excess, proportional to the triangle's area. A flat triangle would sit exactly at 180°.

activities.anchor: The first family of circle theorems (E4.7)
activities.caption: call the inscribed angle
activities.name: aaInscribedEst

config.prompt: A chord subtends 100° at the centre of a circle. What angle does it subtend at a point on the major arc?
config.why: The inscribed angle is half the central angle: 100° / 2 = 50°, and it is the same at every point of the major arc.
config.context: a diameter subtends 180° at the centre, so the angle in a semicircle is 90°

config.prompt: Find the line where the cyclic-quadrilateral arithmetic goes wrong:
lines: A cyclic quadrilateral has three angles 70°, 95° and 110°.
Opposite angles of a cyclic quadrilateral sum to 180°.
The remaining angle must pair with 95°: 180° − 95° = 85°.
config.correction: The fourth angle is 85°, not 95° — the angle paired with 95° is forced to 180° − 95°.
config.why: Each opposite pair sums to 180°: 70° + 110° and 95° + 85°.

activities.caption: pair each geometry with its invariants
activities.name: aaGeomMatch

config.prompt: Pair each geometry with what its group of transformations preserves:

pairs.right: collinearity and ratios along a line

config.why: Klein's Erlangen programme: choose the transformation group, and the geometry is the study of its invariants.

activities.anchor: The deepest marriage of the two halves of this page
activities.caption: true or false — symmetry decides solvability
activities.name: aaGaloisJudge

statements.s: The general quintic is unsolvable by radicals because its symmetry group S₅ contains A₅, a simple group with no suitable chain of subgroups.
statements.why: Solvability by radicals corresponds to a chain of nested normal subgroups; A₅ blocks such a chain.

statements.s: Galois theory says a polynomial is solvable by radicals exactly when its symmetry group is abelian.
statements.why: The group must be solvable, not necessarily abelian — abelian is sufficient but not necessary.

statements.s: The same theory decides which regular polygons are constructible with ruler and compasses.
statements.why: Constructibility reduces to nested square roots, a condition on the Galois group.
